otp_summary: The DDR3 SDRAM die itself does not expose a normative OTP / fuse register at the bus interface. JESD79-3C standardizes only the DRAM component (volatile DRAM array + four Mode Registers that must be re-programmed after each power cycle). The OTP-equivalent for DDR3 lives on the DIMM module as the SPD (Serial Presence Detect) EEPROM, a 256-byte (DDR3 UDIMM/SODIMM) or 512-byte (DDR3 RDIMM/LRDIMM) I2C-attached EEPROM defined by JEDEC JESD21-C Annex K. The SPD is factory-programmed by the DIMM manufacturer and is read by the host BIOS at boot via SMBus.

spd_eeprom_layout_summary.device: I2C EEPROM at address 0x50..0x57 on SMBus
spd_eeprom_layout_summary.spec_reference: JESD21-C Annex K — Serial Presence Detect for DDR3 SDRAM Modules

factory_programmed_dram_die_metadata: The DRAM die may carry vendor-internal trim fuses and stepping ID, but these are not exposed at the bus interface and are not normative in JESD79-3C.
permanent_state_after_power_off: DRAM array contents are volatile (lost on VDD removal). MR0-MR3 are also volatile and must be re-programmed on every power-up. The SPD EEPROM contents on the DIMM ARE non-volatile (factory OTP-equivalent) but accessed via the separate SMBus / I2C interface, not via the DDR3 command bus.
notes: From the controller / host's perspective, the SPD is the canonical 'OTP fingerprint' of a DDR3 DIMM — manufacturer ID, model, capacity, supported speed bins, timing parameters, organization, voltage, optional feature support are all read from SPD at boot. JEDEC JESD21-C Annex K is the definitive document for the SPD layout; this layer (L11) summarizes the key fields a host BIOS / controller IP must parse.
